```{=html}
</div>
```

## Plain English Summary

::: lang-en
Detecting early memory and thinking problems is important — but 
cognitive testing typically requires trained staff, specialist 
equipment, and a clinic visit. This limits how widely and how often 
such assessments can be carried out, particularly in rural areas or 
settings with limited resources.

The Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus (OCS-Plus) is a tablet-based 
cognitive test that has been validated across several patient 
populations. However, it still requires a trained clinician to 
administer it. To make cognitive screening more scalable and 
accessible, a fully automated version — the 
[MEYOCS-plus](https://meytec.de/meyocs-plus/) — was developed in 
collaboration with the medical technology company Meytec. The 
MEYOCS-plus can be completed independently by the user, with no 
clinical staff required during the assessment itself.

I contributed to this development process as one of the neuropsychological 
experts on the project, working closely with Meytec's programmers to 
translate the original test tasks into a fully automated format. This 
involved drafting detailed task specifications, reviewing 
implementations, and ensuring that the automated version preserved the 
scientific and clinical integrity of the original instrument.

The MEYOCS-plus has since become the foundation of an ongoing research project ([TEAM project](https://www.uniklinikum-jena.de/Uniklinikum+Jena/Aktuelles/Archiv/PM_Archiv+2024/Demenzerkrankungen+fr%C3%BChzeitig+erkennen+und+therapieren-pos-0.html)), which is evaluating the tool in real-world 
settings, including rural healthcare environments, with the goal of 
identifying people at early risk for memory problems and connecting them 
with specialist care.

The MEYOCSplus has also been used in further studies
examining cognitive symptoms in patients with liver disease and
Parkinson's disease, further demonstrating its versatility across
different patient populations.
:::

::: lang-de
Die frühzeitige Erkennung von Gedächtnis- und Denkproblemen ist 
wichtig – doch kognitive Tests erfordern in der Regel geschultes 
Personal, spezielle Geräte und einen Klinikbesuch. Dies schränkt 
ein, wie breit und wie häufig solche Untersuchungen durchgeführt 
werden können, insbesondere in ländlichen Gebieten oder 
ressourcenarmen Umgebungen.

Der Oxford Cognitive Screen-Plus (OCS-Plus) ist ein tabletbasierter 
kognitiver Test, der für verschiedene Patientengruppen validiert 
wurde. Er erfordert jedoch nach wie vor eine klinisch geschulte 
Fachkraft für die Durchführung. Um kognitives Screening skalierbarer 
und zugänglicher zu machen, wurde in Zusammenarbeit mit dem 
Medizintechnikunternehmen Meytec eine vollständig automatisierte 
Version entwickelt – der 
[MEYOCS-plus](https://meytec.de/meyocs-plus/). Der MEYOCS-plus kann 
von den Nutzerinnen und Nutzern selbstständig bearbeitet werden, 
ohne dass während der Testung klinisches Personal anwesend sein muss.

Ich war an diesem Entwicklungsprozess als neuropsychologische 
Fachexpertin beteiligt und arbeitete eng mit den Programmierern von 
Meytec zusammen, um die ursprünglichen Testaufgaben in ein 
vollständig automatisiertes Format zu überführen. Dazu gehörten das 
Verfassen detaillierter Aufgabenbeschreibungen, die Überprüfung der 
Umsetzungen sowie die Sicherstellung, dass die automatisierte Version 
die wissenschaftliche und klinische Qualität des Originalinstruments 
beibehält.

Der MEYOCS-plus bildet inzwischen die Grundlage eines laufenden Forschungsprojekts ([TEAM-Projekts](https://www.uniklinikum-jena.de/Uniklinikum+Jena/Aktuelles/Archiv/PM_Archiv+2024/Demenzerkrankungen+fr%C3%BChzeitig+erkennen+und+therapieren-pos-0.html)), das das Verfahren in 
realen Versorgungsumgebungen, einschließlich ländlicher 
Gesundheitseinrichtungen, erprobt. Ziel ist es, Menschen mit einem 
frühen Risiko für Gedächtnisveränderungen zu identifizieren und sie 
an spezialisierte Versorgungsangebote weiterzuvermitteln.

Der MEYOCSplus wurde zudem in weiteren Studien zur Erfassung
kognitiver Symptome bei Patientinnen und Patienten mit Lebererkrankungen
und Morbus Parkinson eingesetzt und zeigt damit seine Einsatzbreite
über verschiedene Patientengruppen hinaus.
:::

## For Researchers

**Status:** [Ongoing]{.status-ongoing}

**My role:** Neuropsychological expert for instrument development

**Responsibilities:** Scientific liaison between research team and
industry partner (Meytec); drafting of detailed neuropsychological
task specifications for automated implementation; iterative review
of programmer implementations; conference presentations of
preliminary data at international conferences.

**Development:**
The [MEYOCS-plus](https://meytec.de/meyocs-plus/) is a fully automated 
adaptation of the tablet-based OCS-Plus, developed in collaboration 
with Meytec to enable standardised cognitive screening with minimal 
personnel requirements. Development involved close translation of 
established OCS-Plus tasks into a self-administered digital format, 
with particular attention to preserving psychometric properties and 
clinical validity. The instrument targets low-threshold deployment 
in settings where traditional neuropsychological assessment is 
impractical, including telemedicine and rural care contexts.

**TEAM Project - Translational Implementation:**
The MEYOCS-plus is now the basis of an independent PhD project 
(TEAM project) examining its real-world application. The study 
deploys the tool in rural healthcare settings to identify individuals 
at risk for MCI, with a structured referral pathway to 
specialist assessment at the Memory Centre, Department of Neurology, 
Jena University Hospital. Clinical validation uses algorithm-based 
classification confirmed against the CERAD battery. Normative data 
are being established in a sample of over 300 healthy adults.

**Further Clinical Applications:**

The MEYOCS-plus has been deployed in two additional studies,
in which I contributed as neuropsychological expert and manuscript
co-author.

*Hepatic encephalopathy in liver cirrhosis:* A prospective study
of 103 patients at Jena University Hospital examined whether the
MEYOCS-plus can detect minimal hepatic encephalopathy (HE), a common
but diagnostically challenging complication of liver cirrhosis.
The tool was successfully administered in 95 patients and showed
significant deviations from normative values in memory, attention,
and processing speed subtests, with results correlating well with
established psychometric measures. Manuscript in preparation.

*Cognitive deficits in Parkinson's disease:* A feasibility and
validity study in 50 patients with clinically confirmed Parkinson's
disease examined the MEYOCS-plus as a screening tool for cognitive
deficit profiles. All participants successfully completed the
assessment. Cluster analysis revealed three distinct cognitive
deficit profiles. Results support the MEYOCS-plus as a practical and
accepted instrument for domain-specific cognitive screening in
Parkinson's patients. Manuscript in preparation.

**Publications:** Manuscripts in preparation.
